Aerial Wildlife Survey Report
Pronghorn Survey Antelope Management Areas C, E, F, G (2024)
Classification: Public
Background
Aerial surveys for pronghorn have been conducted in 
Alberta since 1963. In 1985 a trend block survey was 
developed to sample portions of primary range in each 
antelope management area (AMA) in the province (see 
Table 1 for WMUs and area of each AMA). For a full survey, 
approximately 17% of the 37,544 km2 of primary antelope 
range in the province is flown to provide information on 
population densities and herd composition both within 
AMAs and provincially. From 2007-2012, pronghorn surveys 
were conducted by the Alberta Conservation Association 
(ACA) and summary results can be found on their website 
at http://www.ab-conservation.com/programs/wildlife/
big-game-surveys .
Pronghorn hunting opportunities are in high demand in 
Alberta, making the information collected during aerial surveys 
a critical component of pronghorn management. This report 
provides detailed results of the survey conducted by Alberta 
Environment and Protected Areas in 2024, and summarizes 
pronghorn trends within surveyed AMAs from 2013-2021. 
Additionally, a pilot roadside survey is reported where roadside 
observations were used to derive buck:doe and fawn:doe ratios 
and compared to results from the aerial survey.
Survey Method
The survey was flown in an AS350 SD2 aircraft July 13-16, 
2024. Each AMA contains from one to seven designated 
survey blocks (Figure 1) with 1.6 km wide fixed strip transects 
spaced 3.2-6.4 km apart. At each observation point animals 
were counted and classified as bucks, does, or fawns. 
Pronghorn density (#observed/km 2) within each AMA was 
calculated by dividing number of animals observed on 
transect by search area (sum of transect lengths multiplied 
by 1.6 km). For a population estimate within each AMA flown, 
the observed density was multiplied by the area of the AMA. 
AMA G also contain portions of secondary range that was 
not surveyed. Density of pronghorn in secondary range is 
estimated as 0.04/km2, which was added to the population 
estimate within primary range of AMA G. Buck and fawn:doe 
ratios were calculated for each AMA as #bucks or fawns 
observed / #does observed.
Roadside buck:doe and fawn:doe assessments were 
conducted in six of eight AMAs with ratios calculated as 
above. Staff scanned an area within roughly 200 m of roads 
and stopped at locations where pronghorn were enountered. 
GPS location, number of bucks, does and fawns was 
recorded. AMAs C and F were specifically targeted, but 
one route encompassed most of pronghorn range with the 
exception of AMAs E and H.

Results 
Aerial Survey: In 2024 AMAs C, E, F, and G were flown for a 
total linear survey effort of 1,922 km, and was 3,075 km2 of an 
estimated 21,352 km2 within those AMAs (14%). Secondary 
range in AMA G is approximately 2,121 km2. That contributes 
an estimated 82 animals to the overall total in AMA G. Among 
the four AMAs surveyed, 1,623 pronghorn were observed 
on-transect; 971 doe, 392 buck, and 260 fawn. The combined 
buck:doe and fawn:doe ratios were 0.40 and 0.27, respectively 
(Table 1). Since only four of the eight AMAs were surveyed, a 
provincial estimate was not achieved. The highest population 
density occurred in AMA E (0.59 pronghorn/km2), while 
buck:doe and fawn:doe ratios were highest in AMA G (0.59 and 
0.31, respectively; Table 1). The combined population estimates 
of the four AMAs surveyed was 10,253, a 14% increase over 
the last aerial survey in 2021 (Figure 1). Combined buck:doe 
ratios were relatively stable, but there was a marked decrease 
in fawn:doe ratios since the last survey (Figure 2). Increases in 
abundance compared to the 2021 survey of 63%, 43%, and 
23% occurred in AMAs C, E, and G, respectively, while there 
was a 22% decline in AMA F. Those increases were primarily 
a result of increased doe abundance. A decrease in fawn:doe 
ratios was observed in all AMAs surveyed (Table 1), indicating 
poor recruitment in 2024.

Roadside Age/Sex Classification: Four staff each drove 
a route varying in linear distance from 172 km to 1764 km. 
Two routes focused on trend blocks in AMA F, one on trend 
block in AMA C, and one that did not focus on trend blocks 
but covered 1784 km over 6 AMAs (excluded AMA H and 
E). Overall, 2531 km were surveyed from roadside in six 
AMAs and 449 pronghorn were observed. That represents 
28% of detections in 1922 km of aerial surveys, certainly a 
result of greater visibility from aircraft. The overall buck:doe 
and fawn:doe ratios were 0.53 and 0.34, respectively, a 
substantially higher buck:doe ratio, but similar fawn:doe ratio 
to those observed in aerial surveys from AMAs C, E, F, and G 
(0.40 and 0.27; Table 1). Buck:doe and fawn:doe ratios over 
the 1764 km route were 0.43 and 0.34 respectively, similar to 
those observed in aerial surveys of C, E, F and G combined 
(Table 1). Unfortunately, those results are not directly 
comparable in a management context, since additional AMAs 
were surveyed on that route (AMAs A, B, D) and AMA E 
was excluded, but shows that over large geographic scales 
roadside surveys can provide supplemental information on 
general age/sex trends when aerial surveys are lacking.

For more direct comparisons with aerial survey data, roadside 
data was partitioned by AMA, and management areas other 
than those surveyed by aircraft were excluded (Figure 3). It is 
clear that while linear distances surveyed from roadside and 
aircraft were more or less comparable, the number of animals 
observed and classified from aircraft far exceeded detection 
from the road. Further, when partitioned by AMA, buck:doe 
and fawn:doe ratios from roadside can be misleading. AMA C 
and F showed a strong bias of buck detections from roadside, 
while fawn:doe ratios tended to be higher in all AMAs from 
roadside as compared to aerial surveys (Figure 4). These 
results indicate that higher linear distances travelled by road 
in each AMA are required to achieve age/sex classifications 
consistent with aerial surveys. A logistical challenge in 
achieving that is the relatively low road density in many areas 
of pronghorn primary range in Alberta.
